stories.title: Nepal declines foreign rescue help, South Korea says it is 'negotiating'
stories.summary: Nepal does not need foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations following the devastating flash flood that swept through several towns, its foreign ministry said on Friday, despite offers of help from several countries with nationals missing in the disaster. The flood tore through areas including Rasuwa district near the Chinese border, levelling entire towns, damaging hydropower projects and killing close to 500 people. Hundreds of foreign nationals are still missing, including from South Korea, which said it has already sent a response team to Nepal and will also dispatch a disaster relief team. But Nepal's foreign ministry said on Friday that it was managing the rescue efforts. "The offer for help is natural. Our security agencies are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help," Lok Bahadur Chhetri, spokesperson for the foreign ministry, said without providing further details. South Korea's foreign ministry said Nepal had indicated it was not yet planning to accept foreign rescue teams. "South Korea will keep negotiating with Nepal over the matter," the ministry added. Seoul has pledged $1 million in humanitarian assistance through international organisations, its foreign minister said on X. Nine South Koreans working in a hydropower plant were missing and 10 were stranded, South Korea's foreign ministry said on Wednesday. The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the United States, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search-and-rescue teams to assist in the operation.

stories.title: Nepal will need billions for flood recovery, minister says
stories.summary: Nepal needs at least a few billion dollars for flood recovery after flash floods killed 469 people and destroyed infrastructure near the China border. The government is providing rescue, temporary shelter, and basic needs while international bodies and neighbouring countries offer aid. Nepal plans a major fundraising campaign and will consult the IMF on financial impacts, while ensuring safety amid risks of a second flood outburst. Nepal will need at least “a few billion dollars” to recover from the devastation caused by flash floods, prompting the US$45 billion (S$57 billion) economy to seek international funding for a massive reconstruction effort, according to Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle. At least 469 people have been confirmed dead, a toll that is expected to rise in the coming days after flash floods sent an avalanche of rock, mud and water through a Nepalese valley near the border with China, wiping out bridges, roads and entire settlements. More than 1,500 people are missing across Nepal and China, including visitors from India, Malaysia, Australia, the UK and the US. “Cumulatively, I think the losses and damages when they will be finally quantified in a week or so, will amount to at least a few billion dollars,” Wagle told Haslinda Amin in an interview to Bloomberg Television. “Preliminary estimates are quite worrying.” The finance minister’s comments come after Nepal’s billionaire businessman. Binod Chaudhary told Bloomberg News that he would not be surprised if rebuilding costs hit US$5 billion. His Chaudhary Group spans 12 business verticals, from food and telecom to infrastructure and banking. Nepal has a long experience in dealing with natural disaster as its location in the Himalayas makes it vulnerable to earthquakes, landslides and flash floods.

stories.title: Norway's King Harald dies aged 89
stories.summary: Norway's King Harald V has died at the age of 89, after he was taken to hospital last week for treatment for a rare blood condition. The palace in Oslo said he passed away peacefully at 06:35 local time (04:35GMT) on Friday at the national hospital in Oslo. In the 24 hours leading up to his death, members of the royal family had visited the king, and crowds had laid flowers at the palace. Harald was Norway's first king born in Norway since the 14th Century. He will be succeeded by his son Haakon. After 35 years on the throne, he will be remembered as a popular and reforming figure who modernised the monarchy, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure at Norway's most difficult moments. Royal observers say he was down-to-earth, respected and beloved, describing him as a "grandfather" of the nation and the "People's king" - a title also used by his father King Olav V. In the wake of the 2011 bomb and gun attacks on Oslo and the island of Utøya, Harald appealed to Norwegians to support each other and not "let fear take over". More recently, Harald and his family have faced health challenges and scandal, especially over his daughter-in-law Mette-Marit's association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son Marius Borg Høiby's conviction for rape. During his reign, the Norwegian monarchy became more egalitarian and transparent with finances and health, Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen, historian and TV2 royal correspondent, told the BBC. Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, described the late king as "one of us", while Caroline Vagle, royal expert for Se og Hør magazine, said he had "always been very close to the people". When Norway's national football team returned from the US after making it to the World Cup quarter-finals for the first time, Harald welcomed them home at the palace.

stories.title: China’s ‘Usain Bot’ shows the limits of human speed
stories.summary: Parts of the robot’s torso and waist were redesigned to cut weight and reduce the effort needed.
article_sentences: China's Tiangong Ultra humanoid robot ran 100m in 8.64sec, beating Usain Bolt's 9.58sec human record with a speed of almost 42kmh.
The robot uses shorter, faster steps and electric motors, allowing it to maintain top speed without fatigue, unlike human sprinters.
Despite its speed, Tiangong lacks human-like decision-making and balance, crashing into a wall at the finish and needing better control for future improvements.
A made-in-China humanoid shattered Usain Bolt’s world record time in the 100m sprint this week, a milestone in the development of robots that can match, and even surpass, human achievements.
But the robot did not beat Bolt by running like him, or like any human, sport science experts say.
In its final and fastest run, China’s Tiangong Ultra humanoid ran 100 m in 8.64sec, blazing past Bolt’s 9.58sec human world record.
That amounts to an average speed for the robot of almost 42kmh.

“It is a remarkable advancement in technology where humanoids can keep balance and sprint at a speed that humans can’t catch up with,” said Jung Moon-hyun, a sports science professor at South Korea’s Chungnam National University.

But the differences between Bolt’s closely studied 2009 world-record run in Berlin and the humanoid runs in Beijing also highlight both the power of robots – and the areas, like decision making and perception, where they still lag, other experts said.
Take the start.
Bolt burst from the blocks in Berlin with a lightning-fast reaction time of 0.146sec.
Starting blocks allow human sprinters to generate horizontal force at the start of the race to build speed.

stories.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: Nepal tourism faces another setback as Rasuwa disaster exposes mountain risks
stories.summary: Nepal’s exposure to climate-related disasters is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.
article_sentences: The August 26 flash flood in Rasuwa severely disrupted Nepal's tourism, especially the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage, exposing growing risks from climate change in the Himalayan region.

Climate change is increasing the danger of glacial lake outbursts and floods, threatening communities, infrastructure, and tourism, highlighting the need for better disaster preparedness and sustainable tourism policies.

Nepal's tourism has shown resilience through past crises, but new challenges from climate-induced hazards demand advanced technology, early-warning systems, and international support to protect the mountain environment and economy.
Nepal’s tourism industry was entering its peak season in September 2025 when the Gen Z-led anti-corruption protests brought the sector to a sudden halt.
The unrest came after years of setbacks.

Before that, catastrophic floods had battered the country, two major aviation accidents had raised fresh concerns about air safety, and the Covid-19 pandemic had brought international tourism to a standstill.
Now, another disaster has struck at a particularly vulnerable time.
The devastating flash flood that swept through Rasuwa on Aug 26 has shattered hopes of a strong tourism recovery, particularly for the lucrative Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage market.
The disaster struck the Rasuwagadhi-Timure area, a major gateway for pilgrims travelling from Nepal to Tibet.
More importantly, it has raised a much bigger question for Nepal’s tourism-dependent economy: are the country’s mountains becoming an increasingly dangerous destination because of climate change?
A full assessment of Aug 26’s disaster is under way.

But the destruction has already highlighted the potentially devastating consequences of glacial outbursts and other climate-induced hazards for communities, infrastructure and tourists in the Himalayan region.
